source_note: Lee, 'Analysis of Success Probabilities in Field Hockey with Machine Learning', Wharton Sports Analytics Journal 2024 (Jethro R. Lee, Northeastern University), 19 pages. Mixed-effects logistic regression of goal-scoring probability on Northeastern's 2023 field hockey season (18 matches/19 players/270 shots/117 penalty corners/50 goals), fit in glmer (Laplace) and RStan (Bayesian hierarchical); player random effects interacted with penalty-corner indicator to capture strategic intentional misses (coaching insight); small-sample shrinkage; glmer-vs-RStan Score.Difference sign discrepancy; future nested bivariate binomial model + simulation validation + overfitting guard. Extracted faithfully (not a derivative summary). Equations 1 (Bayes), 2/4 (logit link), 3 (home odds ratio) are printed in a shifted/custom font that extracts garbled; reconstructed in labeled LaTeX and flagged here and in assumptions. Math-italic Greek (beta/theta) interspersed in prose; quotes selected from clean spans. Domain math (sports ML) matches catalog; field hockey, not football. The hierarchical player-ability random effects, difficulty-contextualized credit, intent-vs-outcome attribution, small-sample shrinkage, and cross-estimator sign-discrepancy veto are sport-agnostic and directly isomorphic to GSE's player-valuation and credit-attribution layer. No sportsbook lines/spreads/totals/implied odds in source or lifted into GSE.

primitives.name: Field hockey is an understudied sport-analytics application
primitives.verbatim_quote: Field hockey is a sport that has thus far been understudied
assumptions: Field hockey is a relatively unexplored application of sports analytics; the project uses play-by-play data to inform on-field decisions, evaluate factors leading teams/players to perform better or worse, and assess the on-field value of events (penalty corners, goals) especially on a player basis, drawing on nested success-probability work in baseball and ice hockey.

layer2.mapping: The understudied-sport gap is the same novel-application opportunity GSE identifies for transferring analytics methods.
layer2.telemetry: field hockey understudied; PBP -> player value; nested success prob (baseball/ice hockey precedent)

primitives.name: Goal: predict players' ability to score under different conditions
primitives.verbatim_quote: building a model to predict players' ability to score under different conditions
assumptions: The main goal is to use modern machine learning to analyze field hockey player performance, building a model to predict players' ability to score under different conditions (match location, score difference, penalty-corner situation) and estimate random effects capturing individual players' likelihood to score.

layer2.mapping: Condition-dependent scoring prediction is the same situational player-value model GSE builds.
layer2.telemetry: predict goal-scoring under conditions (location/score diff/PC); player random effects

primitives.name: Prototype mixed-effects logistic regression in glmer (Laplace) and RStan (Bayesian)
primitives.verbatim_quote: implemented a prototype mixed effects logistic regression model with both glmer
assumptions: A prototype mixed-effects logistic regression model is implemented in both glmer (lme4, Laplace approximation) and RStan (Bayesian hierarchical), with outputs compared; the model investigates match location, score difference, and penalty-corner situational effects plus player random effects interacted with the penalty-corner indicator.

layer2.mapping: The dual-implementation mixed-effects model is the same cross-check GSE runs between frequentist and Bayesian fits.
layer2.telemetry: mixed-effects logistic; glmer (Laplace) + RStan (Bayesian); compared

primitives.name: Northeastern 2023: 18 matches, 19 players, 270 shots, 117 penalty corners, 50 goals
primitives.verbatim_quote: the model was able to use data from 18 field hockey matches and 19 hockey players, which included 270 shots, 117 penalty corners, and 50 goals
assumptions: Play-by-play data scraped from Northeastern's field hockey website with Python Pandas, mapping game time to events (goal, penalty corner, assist), with home/away, score difference, and penalty-corner-to-shot manually recorded; one season yields 18 matches, 19 players, 270 shots, 117 penalty corners, and 50 goals.

layer2.mapping: The scraped single-season dataset is the same small-sample event-data construction GSE uses for player models.
layer2.telemetry: Northeastern 2023; Pandas scrape; 18 matches/19 players/270 shots/117 PC/50 goals

primitives.name: One season/team kept homogeneous so random effects measure within-season average
primitives.verbatim_quote: Only one season and one team (Northeastern University) were investigated due to time constraints
assumptions: Only one season and one team (Northeastern) were investigated due to time constraints and to eliminate the need to account for a player's scoring aptitude varying between seasons; keeping data homogeneous ensures the random effects best measure each player's average performance within a season.

layer2.mapping: The homogeneity-for-random-effects design is the same variance-control GSE applies to isolate player ability.
layer2.telemetry: 1 season/1 team; homogeneous -> random effects = within-season average ability

primitives.name: Model 0 drawback: assumes all players equally proficient except noise
primitives.verbatim_quote: it assumes all players in the data set are equally proficient at goal scoring except for random noise
assumptions: Model 0 is a baseline fixed-effects logistic regression where logit(p_lt) is the goal probability, each z term a parameter (score difference, home/away, location, assists, blocks) and each beta its effect, with an intercept bias term; its drawback is assuming all players are equally proficient at goal scoring except for random noise.

layer2.mapping: The fixed-effects-only baseline is the same no-player-heterogeneity model GSE upgrades with random effects.
layer2.telemetry: Model 0: logit(p)=intercept+sum beta*z; assumes equal player proficiency

primitives.name: Model 1: player random effects adjust for ability differences
primitives.verbatim_quote: we can adjust for the likely differences in player ability by including random effects for players
assumptions: Model 1 adds player random effects (a terms) that alter how parameter values affect each individual's goal-scoring logit; players who miss shots the model classifies as more difficult receive less harsh negative impacts than players who miss easier shots, contextualizing missed-shot credit by shot difficulty.

layer2.mapping: Difficulty-contextualized random effects are the same shot-quality-adjusted player credit GSE assigns.
layer2.telemetry: Model 1: player random effects a; miss difficult shot -> less penalty than miss easy shot

primitives.name: Coaching insight: some players intentionally miss PC shots to force rebounds
primitives.verbatim_quote: certain players take shots directly after penalty corners not intending to score, but rather to force the ball to rebound to a player in a better position
assumptions: A discussion with the Northeastern coaching staff revealed that certain players take shots directly after penalty corners not intending to score but to force the ball to rebound to a player in a better position, so some players perform better from the field of play than immediately following penalty corners; the player-by-penalty-corner interaction captures this strategic intent.

layer2.mapping: Strategic-intent-vs-outcome is literally GSE's credit-attribution problem: a missed shot may be a deliberate play, not a failure.
layer2.telemetry: intentional PC miss -> rebound to better position; intent != outcome; interaction captures

primitives.name: Two random effects per player: PC set-play vs all other shots
primitives.verbatim_quote: there are now two per player; one which estimates the player's goal-scoring performance on penalty corner set plays, and one which estimates their goal-scoring performance on all other shots
assumptions: The player-by-Shot.after.PC interaction adds a second set of random effects, giving two per player: one estimating goal-scoring on penalty-corner set plays and one on all other shots; implemented in glmer as (1 | Player:Shot.after.PC) and in RStan as a two-column matrix per player (Shot.after.PC FALSE/TRUE).

layer2.mapping: The situation-split random effects are the same context-conditioned player valuation GSE uses.
layer2.telemetry: 2 random effects/player: PC vs non-PC; glmer (1|Player:Shot.after.PC); RStan 2-col matrix

primitives.name: glmer (lme4) uses Laplace approximation for betas + random effects
primitives.verbatim_quote: The first package is lme4, to employ the glmer function, which uses a numerical approximation technique (i.e., Laplace approximation)
assumptions: The first implementation uses lme4's glmer function, which employs a numerical approximation technique (Laplace approximation) to obtain beta values and random effects; the author's intuition is that Laplace approximation would be more beneficially complex to implement for the intended final bivariate binomial model than Bayesian RStan.

layer2.mapping: The Laplace-approximation fit is the same fast frequentist mixed-model estimator GSE compares against MCMC.
layer2.telemetry: glmer/lme4; Laplace approximation for beta + random effects

primitives.name: RStan: player scoring prior normal(mean 0, variance sigma^2)
primitives.verbatim_quote: the prior distribution on each player's scoring probability is normal with a mean of 0 and variance
assumptions: In RStan the prior on each player's scoring probability is normal with mean 0 and variance sigma-squared, initially assigning every player average goal-scoring propensity; the model then adjusts each player's probability according to the data (time, penalty corner, home advantage, player random effects) to produce a posterior.

layer2.mapping: The shrinkage-to-average prior is the same hierarchical regularization GSE uses for player effects.
layer2.telemetry: RStan prior: player scoring ~ N(0, sigma^2); start average, update to posterior

primitives.name: Variance hyperprior uniform(0, 10)
primitives.verbatim_quote: a hyperprior distribution that is uniform from 0 to 10
assumptions: The variance sigma-squared of the player prior is given a hyperprior distribution uniform from 0 to 10, a weakly-informative bound on the between-player variance in the Bayesian hierarchical model.

layer2.mapping: The variance hyperprior is the same hierarchical variance regularization GSE specifies.

primitives.name: Time-bin coefficients increase: Northeastern scores more as time passes
primitives.verbatim_quote: The coefficients generally increase as match_seconds_bin holds larger values, meaning the Northeastern team tends to score more goals as time passes
assumptions: The match_seconds_bin coefficients generally increase with larger time bins (glmer 0.3425 to 1.0188; RStan 6.61 to 7.14), meaning Northeastern tends to score more goals as time passes, except for overtime; time is binned into sixths of a match to capture non-linear time effects and interacted with score difference.

primitives.verbatim_quote: we can disregard the overtime data as outlier data
assumptions: The overtime coefficient (3600-4360 seconds) is -14.2380 in glmer with a very large standard error and p-value 0.99196, and -77.38 in RStan with extreme standard deviation 65.97, so the overtime data are disregarded as outliers.

primitives.name: glmer vs RStan Score.Difference sign discrepancy (+1.1885 vs -1.45)
primitives.verbatim_quote: In the RStan model, the Score.Difference parameter is negative (-1.45) while the Shot.after.PC coefficient is also negative (-0.19), indicating a discrepancy between the two models
assumptions: The glmer Score.Difference coefficient is positive (1.1885) while RStan's is negative (-1.45), a discrepancy needing address; both agree Shot.after.PC is negative (glmer -0.2258, RStan -0.19) and that Score.Difference matters more than Shot.after.PC; the glmer sign better aligns with the data except when Northeastern is very behind (3-4 points) where goal proportion peaked, possibly explaining the inconsistency.

primitives.name: Shot conversion: 20.468% non-PC vs 15.152% PC (1 goal per 6.667 PC shots)
primitives.verbatim_quote: the Northeastern team scored about 20.468% of its shots not after penalty corners. In comparison, it only scored about 15.152% of its shots after penalty corners
assumptions: Northeastern scored about 20.468% of shots not after penalty corners versus only 15.152% after penalty corners, so 1/0.152 = 6.667 penalty-corner shots per goal; both models agree players have a better chance scoring not off a penalty corner.

layer2.mapping: The penalty-corner conversion gap is the same set-play efficiency metric GSE tracks.

primitives.name: Coach benchmark: world-class teams score 1 goal per 3 penalty corners
primitives.verbatim_quote: The Northeastern hockey coach reported that world-class teams score 1 goal for every 3 penalty corners
assumptions: The Northeastern hockey coach reported that world-class teams score 1 goal for every 3 penalty corners, versus Northeastern's 1 per 6.667; the player random-effect insights are hoped to help improve penalty-corner performance toward world-class standards.

layer2.mapping: The world-class benchmark is the same external performance target GSE uses to grade a unit.

primitives.name: Random effects correctly shrink 1.000 proportions from 1-shot players
primitives.verbatim_quote: both the glmer and RStan models were able to correctly discern that Player 1 and Player 4's goal proportions of 1.000 for shots not off penalty corners are not comparable due to a lack of data
assumptions: Players 1 and 4 each made only 1 non-penalty-corner shot which happened to be a goal, giving a 1.000 proportion; both glmer and RStan correctly discerned these proportions are not comparable due to lack of data, with random effects near 0 representing average ability and/or minimal data — the hierarchical shrinkage prevents small-sample overrating.

layer2.mapping: Small-sample shrinkage is literally GSE's defense against overrating a player on tiny samples.

primitives.name: Strategic missers (6, 13) poor on PC but near-average on other shots
primitives.verbatim_quote: while due to strategic reasons they are considered poor scorers after penalty corners, on all other shots, they are much closer to average in ability
assumptions: Players 6 and 13 occasionally take bad shots after penalty corners for strategic purposes; Player 6's PC random effect is -0.676 (glmer)/-0.79 (RStan) versus non-PC -0.059/0.15, and Player 13's PC -0.377/-0.23 versus non-PC -0.195/-0.02, showing that while strategic reasons make them poor PC scorers, on all other shots they are much closer to average.

primitives.name: Nested model must not treat all PC misses as detrimental (strategic deflections)

assumptions: A shot off a penalty corner can lead to a deflection that some coaches believe better enables scoring than a direct attempt, so the nested probability model should not classify all missed penalty-corner shots as detrimental to a player's goal-scoring probability, and should account for players missing penalty shots for specific strategic reasons.

reasoning_traces.think: The retrocausal genealogy of this paper is the transfer of nested success-probability modeling into a sport that analytics has barely touched. Jethro Lee, writing at Northeastern University for the Wharton Sports Analytics Journal in 2024, observes that field hockey is understudied, and that success probabilities have been modeled extensively in baseball, where a bivariate binomial nests extra-base-hit percentage within batting average, and in ice hockey, where a clean face-off win is more valuable than a mere win. The project scrapes play-by-play data from Northeastern's 2023 field hockey season with Python Pandas, manually recording home versus away, score difference, and whether a penalty corner led to an immediate shot, yielding 18 matches, 19 players, 270 shots, 117 penalty corners, and 50 goals. Only one season and one team are used to keep the data homogeneous so that player random effects measure within-season average ability rather than cross-season variation. The recursive theory of mind is the mixed-effects logistic model and its dual implementation. Model 0 is a fixed-effects logistic regression whose drawback is assuming all players are equally proficient except for noise; Model 1 adds player random effects so that missing a difficult shot penalizes a player less than missing an easy one. Crucially, a discussion with the coaching staff revealed that some players intentionally miss shots directly after penalty corners to force a rebound to a better-positioned teammate, so the model interacts the player random effect with the penalty-corner indicator, producing two random effects per player, one for penalty-corner set plays and one for all other shots. The model is fit both with glmer using Laplace approximation and with RStan using a Bayesian hierarchical model whose player prior is normal with mean zero and a variance given a uniform zero-to-ten hyperprior, run for five chains of three thousand iterations, and Bayes' theorem converts the posterior into the likelihood of scoring given a parameter. Cross-layer veto adjudication is the comparison of the two fits and the handling of unreliable estimates. The time-bin coefficients rise across the match, indicating Northeastern scores more as time passes, but the overtime coefficient is discarded as an outlier given its enormous standard error and p-value near one. The home coefficient is positive in both fits, about 0.56 in glmer and 0.72 in RStan, translating to roughly 2.5 percent more shots scored at home and, via the exponentiated coefficient e to the 0.72 equals 2.054, about twice the scoring odds at home. The most important disagreement is the score-difference coefficient, positive 1.1885 in glmer but negative 1.45 in RStan, a sign flip the author attributes to Northeastern's goal proportion peaking when very far behind; both fits agree the penalty-corner coefficient is negative and that score difference matters more than the penalty-corner indicator. The implementation invariants map directly onto GSE. The player random effects are GSE's hierarchical player-ability estimates; the difficulty-contextualized miss penalty is GSE's shot-quality-adjusted credit; the intentional-miss interaction is GSE's intent-versus-outcome attribution; the small-sample shrinkage that correctly refuses to rate Players 1 and 4 highly on a single made shot each is GSE's defense against tiny-sample overrating; and the glmer-versus-RStan sign discrepancy is GSE's model-disagreement veto. The outputs are goal-scoring probabilities and player random effects from play-by-play data; GSE lifts no sportsbook lines, spreads, totals, or implied odds. The conversion gap is concrete: Northeastern scores 20.468 percent of non-penalty-corner shots versus 15.152 percent of penalty-corner shots, one goal per 6.667 penalty-corner shots against the coach's world-class benchmark of one per three. The caveats close the account with the strategic-miss nuance and the overfitting guard. Players 6 and 13 have markedly negative penalty-corner random effects but near-average non-penalty-corner effects, confirming they are strategic missers rather than poor scorers, so the future nested bivariate binomial model must not classify all penalty-corner misses as detrimental, since a miss can create a deflection opportunity. That nested model, which chains the probability of shooting off a penalty corner into the probability of scoring from it, has been validated by simulating fake data and checking that pre-defined parameters are recovered, and the planned addition of field-location random effects is explicitly constrained by the risk of overfitting too many parameters to too little data. The invariant for GSE is to carry the mixed-effects player-valuation pipeline, the intent-aware credit attribution, and the small-sample shrinkage while recording the cross-estimator sign discrepancy, the overtime outlier exclusion, and the overfitting guard before any quantitative reuse, treating a deliberate missed shot as a play to be understood rather than a failure to be penalized. Two further details sharpen the GSE transfer. The time-by-score-difference interaction itself flips sign between the fits, negative in glmer, meaning that within each sixth of a match Northeastern scores fewer goals as it gets further ahead, but positive in RStan, another instance of the cross-estimator disagreement that bars a confident directional claim; and the blocked-or-goal-after-block coefficient is negative in both fits, about minus 1.39 in glmer and minus 1.84 in RStan, indicating Northeastern is better at scoring from unblocked shots. The planned field-location extension would divide the field into six zones and add a player-by-location interaction to locate each player's most and least efficient scoring areas, but the author explicitly flags the overfitting danger of multiplying random effects against a small dataset. The RStan appendix also shows weak convergence for some parameters, with large standard deviations and low effective sample sizes, an honest caveat that the Bayesian fit is not uniformly well-mixed. For GSE these reinforce the same discipline: treat cross-estimator sign flips as vetoes, prefer the simpler model when data are thin, and report convergence quality rather than presenting a posterior as settled.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Transfer nested success-prob modeling to understudied field hockey. Jethro Lee, Northeastern, Wharton Sports Analytics Journal 2024. Precedent: baseball bivariate binomial (extra-base hit nested in batting avg, Han 2022 Entropy); ice hockey clean face-off win (Czuzoj-Shulman 2019). Scraped Northeastern 2023 PBP (Pandas) + manual home/away/score-diff/PC-to-shot; 18 matches/19 players/270 shots/117 PC/50 goals. One season/team for homogeneity (random effects = within-season avg). Mixed-effects logistic: Model 0 fixed (equal-proficiency drawback), Model 1 + player random effects interacted w/ Shot.after.PC (2 per player). glmer (Laplace) + RStan (Bayesian, N(0,sigma^2) prior, sigma^2~U(0,10), 5 chains x 3000).
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Covariates: Home/Shot.after.PC/Blocked.or.goal.after.block (indicators), match_seconds_bin (binned sixths 0-4360), Score.Difference (numeric), time x score-diff interaction. glmer (1|Player:Shot.after.PC); RStan 2-col matrix. Bayes Eq1 P(Y|theta)=P(theta|Y)P(Y)/P(theta); logit Eq2/4 log(p/(1-p))=a+sum beta_i X_i; odds Eq3 e^0.72=2.05443. Time-bin coeffs rise (glmer .3425-1.0188/RStan 6.61-7.14); overtime outlier (glmer -14.238 p=.99196/RStan -77.38 SD 65.97) discarded. Home glmer .5611/RStan .72 (~2.5% more, ~2x odds). Equations shifted-font reconstructed. Blocked.or.goal.after.block negative both fits (glmer -1.3918/RStan -1.84): better at unblocked goals.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: glmer vs RStan Score.Difference SIGN FLIP (+1.1885 vs -1.45); Shot.after.PC both neg (-.2258/-.19); trailing-3/4 goal-proportion peak explains. Conversion non-PC 20.468% vs PC 15.152% (1/6.667); world-class 1/3 (coach). Small-sample shrinkage: Player 1/4 1-shot 1.000 not comparable (random effects ~0). Strategic missers Player 6 (PC -.676/-.79 vs non-PC -.059/.15) & 13 (PC -.377/-.23 vs non-PC -.195/-.02) near-average off-PC. Future nested bivariate binomial (PC->goal) must NOT treat all PC misses detrimental (deflection); simulation parameter-recovery validated; player x location overfitting guard (little data). Zero sportsbook lines lifted.

universal_lens: A mixed-effects logistic regression fit in both glmer (Laplace) and RStan (Bayesian) models field-hockey goal-scoring probability from match location, score difference, time, and penalty-corner situation, with two player random effects per athlete (penalty-corner vs other shots) that capture strategic intentional misses and shrink tiny-sample proportions toward average; the two fits agree on most effects but flip the score-difference sign, and the conversion gap (20.5% non-penalty-corner vs 15.2% penalty-corner) is benchmarked against a world-class one-goal-per-three-penalty-corners standard.
gsi_mapping: GSI treats Model 0 fixed logistic (equal-proficiency drawback) -> Model 1 player random effects x Shot.after.PC (2/player; glmer (1|Player:Shot.after.PC), RStan 2-col); Northeastern 2023 18 matches/19 players/270 shots/117 PC/50 goals; covariates Home/Shot.after.PC/Blocked.or.goal.after.block + binned time + Score.Difference + time x score-diff; RStan N(0,sigma^2) prior, sigma^2~U(0,10), 5x3000; Bayes Eq1, logit Eq2/4, odds Eq3 e^0.72=2.05443 (shifted-font reconstructed); time-bin rise, overtime outlier discarded; Home ~2.5%/~2x; Score.Difference glmer +1.1885 vs RStan -1.45 sign flip; conversion 20.468%/15.152% (1/6.667) vs world-class 1/3; Player 1/4 shrinkage; strategic missers 6/13; nested bivariate binomial future + simulation recovery + overfitting guard.
gse_mapping: GSE lifts the hierarchical player-ability random effects, the difficulty-contextualized missed-shot credit, the intent-vs-outcome attribution (strategic penalty-corner misses are plays not failures), the small-sample shrinkage that refuses to overrate single-shot players, and the glmer-vs-RStan sign-discrepancy veto as its player-valuation and credit-attribution layer; records the overtime outlier exclusion, the cross-estimator score-difference sign flip, the nested-model non-detrimental-miss rule, and the parameter-count-vs-data overfitting guard as honest limits; all outputs are goal-scoring probabilities and player random effects from play-by-play data, never sportsbook lines, and a deliberate missed shot is a play to be understood rather than a failure to be penalized.
